I have farmed these 9 mu in Quzhou County for fifty years. I am seventy now, with only a primary schooling, but the land is what I know best. My household has six mouths, and some of my children work in the city, so I cannot take on too much heavy manual labour anymore. I will keep six mu under the wheat‑maize double crop because grain is the backbone of our household—it feeds the family and the livestock, and the harvest can be handled mostly by machine. The remaining three mu I will plant to cotton. Cotton brings in cash, but picking it is back‑breaking work for an old man, so three mu is enough.

For the winter wheat on those six mu, I will plough the field after the maize stalks are cleared and sow my usual improved wheat variety in mid‑October. I will spread compound fertilizer at sowing and then top‑dress with urea at green‑up, altogether about eighteen kg of nitrogen per mu, plus eight kg of phosphate and six kg of potash. My well will give the wheat three irrigations: one before winter to help it establish, one at jointing, and one at flowering. I will spray a herbicide and one fungicide, so two pesticide passes. If the weather is normal I expect about four hundred kg per mu.

Come early June, as soon as the wheat is out, I will rotary till the stubble and sow hybrid maize the same day. Summer maize grows fast in the heat. I will give it sixteen kg of nitrogen per mu, six kg of phosphate, and four kg of potash, using compound and urea as usual. It needs two irrigations from the well—one right after sowing and another when the stems are elongating. Two sprays, herbicide and one for stem borers, will do. I expect around four hundred and sixty kg per mu.

For cotton, I will plough the three mu in spring and sow hybrid Bt cotton at the end of April. I will apply about eighteen kg of nitrogen per mu, seven kg of phosphate, and seven kg of potash. Cotton is thirsty and attracts pests, so I will irrigate three times and spray pesticide four times to keep bollworm and aphids under control. In a decent year that should give me about two hundred and eighty kg of seed cotton per mu.

This is the schedule I have followed for many years. The well water is reliable, the family helps when they are home, and the yields are steady. I see no reason to change what works.
